rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers of v. 30 are promised Gardens of Eden; the recurring image of rivers below the Gardens is discussed at 2:25c.
rows.anchor: The believers described in v. 30 will be rewarded with the Gardens of Eden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse depicts paradisal delights that appear, at least literally, to include gold bracelets and fine green silk garments; related verses mention silver jewelry or silk.
rows.anchor: This verse also describes the joys of the Garden as including what appear to be, at least on a literal level, a set of material or sensual pleasures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many commentators take the Garden's sensual descriptions symbolically rather than literally.
rows.anchor: These sensual descriptions are considered by many commentators to be symbolic, however, and not to be taken literally

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some say the garments are green because green is the color most pleasing to the eye; 55:76 also depicts green cushions in Paradise.
rows.anchor: according to some, this color is the most pleasing to the eye

rows.speaker: Al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī speculates that green silk represents deeds earned, while bracelets are an additional bounty from God.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī speculates that the green silken garments represent what they have earned with their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥadīth say that the extent of a person's Garden ornaments reflects how much they purified themselves through earthly ablutions.
rows.anchor: According to aḥadīth, the extent of one’s ornaments in the Garden reflects the degree to which one has purified oneself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden's couches recur elsewhere in the Quran; some commentators describe them as curtained or canopied.
rows.anchor: The inhabitants of Paradise are also said to be reclining upon couches

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some describe the couches as bejeweled.
rows.anchor: and bejeweled (Q)

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: The gold, silk, and raised couches signal immense luxury in desert Arabia, and some commentators portray the righteous as kings seated on thrones.
rows.anchor: some commentators indicate that these images are meant to suggest that those in Paradise will be like kings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read literally, these delights can seem worldly and materialistic; 43:35 itself describes gold ornaments and couches as worldly enjoyment.
rows.anchor: in 43:35 gold ornaments and couches are described as the enjoyment of the life of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gold and silk are noble luxuries forbidden to Muslim men by several aḥādīth, while women may enjoy them in earthly life; this parallels intoxicants as worldly pleasures reserved for the Hereafter for men.
rows.anchor: there is an analogy between such beverages and gold and silk in that, at least for men, they were pleasures present but forbidden in this world

rows.speaker: Qu, Su
rows.claim: Sufi interpretations read the Garden's luxuries as symbols of witnessing God's Majesty and Beauty and of the righteous' intimacy, love, and union with Him.
rows.anchor: the various luxuries of the Garden as described in the Quran are understood to be symbols of the spiritual joys

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable follows the prominent Makkans' refusal to sit with followers they deemed socially inferior; it warns that prideful ingratitude for worldly blessings ends in their loss.
rows.anchor: follows the discussion of the prominent and wealthy Makkans’ aversion to sitting with those of the Prophet’s followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable's gardens resemble the date-palm and grapevine garden with streams that the Makkans demanded as a condition of believing in the Prophet.
rows.anchor: the gardens as described in this parable are similar to those the Makkans challenged the Prophet to bring forth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grapevines and date palms symbolize both worldly prosperity and Divine Beneficence in the Quran.
rows.anchor: Gardens of grapevines and date palms are emblematic in the Quran of worldly prosperity but also Divine Beneficence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports identify the men as brothers, either Israelites or members of Makhzūm in Makkah; one disbelieving brother invested his inheritance in worldly goods, while the believing brother gave his away in charity.
rows.anchor: Some reports say that the two men were brothers—either two Israelites or two brothers among the Makhzūm clan in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators identify these brothers with the two men debating resurrection in 37:51–60.
rows.anchor: Some commentators suggest that these two brothers are the same two debating resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can mean more literally that the gardens “did him no wrong,” since they produced regularly; this contrasts with the owner wronging himself through pride in v. 35.
rows.anchor: could be translated more literally to mean that the gardens “did him no wrong,” since they produced fruit regularly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamar may mean the gardens' fruit, or “profit,” meaning wealth of various kinds such as gold and silver.
rows.anchor: thamar, here rendered “fruit,” also means“profit,” and may refer to great wealth of various kinds, including gold and silver

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boast of being stronger in men means having more children, especially sons, as well as aides and servants.
rows.anchor: meaning in children, especially sons, as well as aides and servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children signify worldly status, but are not necessarily divine favor and cannot shield one from punishment; disbelievers make that claim at 34:35.
rows.anchor: the Quran warns that these blessings are not necessarily signs of Divine Favor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling disbelief and sin “wronging oneself” is common in the Quran; this man wrongs himself through pride and refusal to acknowledge God as the source of his provision.
rows.anchor: the wealthy man “wrongs himself” through pride and his refusal to acknowledge that his provision comes from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man's confidence that his gardens will never perish exemplifies excessive worldly hope and heedlessness of mortality; all things perish save God's Face, and some who hoard wealth imagine it makes them immortal.
rows.anchor: This delusion points to the moral error of “excessive hope in worldly things”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators read his doubt that the Hour is imminent and conditional return to his Lord as doubt about the Hereafter or his own resurrection.
rows.anchor: commentators understand this and his conditional statement if I am brought back to my Lord to indicate his overall doubt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite uncertainty about resurrection, he expects a better afterlife because he treats wealth and children as personal merit that will endure beyond death.
rows.anchor: he believes that his wealth and good fortune belong to him on the basis of his own personal merit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human origination from dust and then a drop signals human lowliness before God; elsewhere these stages describe human development.
rows.anchor: is understood as an indication of human beings’ lowliness, especially in relation to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fashioning a person as a man means shaping him as a mature individual and endowing him with intelligence and religious responsibility (taklīf).
rows.anchor: Fashioned you as a man refers to God’s having further shaped him as a mature individual

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer recognizes that both poverty and wealth come from God, so he gives thanks in plenty and remains patient in adversity.
rows.anchor: all poverty and wealth comes from God (Q, R) and so is grateful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains elsewhere support and stabilize the earth, but on the Last Day they are set in motion; views say they are removed, made nonexistent, or lifted through the air like clouds.
rows.anchor: some understand this to mean that they will be removed from the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other descriptions say the mountains will be scattered, pulverized, ground up, shifting sand, or carded wool on the Last Day.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere, they are described as scattered (20:105; 77:10); pulverized to powder (56:5); ground up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the earth becomes an open plain because its trees, vegetation, and human constructions are removed.
rows.anchor: Some say that it will be an open plain, because all trees and vegetation as well as all human constructions will be removed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bārizah means coming into clear view or emerging; some interpret it as the dead emerging from their graves for gathering and judgment.
rows.anchor: Open translates bārizah, which comes from a root meaning

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some commentators compare the Judgment ranks to rows formed for prayer; another compares them to rows around the Kaʿbah.
rows.anchor: commentators describe these ranks or rows as similar to those formed for prayer

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Each rank or row may consist of members of one religious community.
rows.anchor: Each rank or row is said to be occupied by a particular religious community

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The phrase may mean people are arrayed in a single line, all visible to one another.
rows.anchor: This phrase may also be translated “arrayed . . . in a row,” that is, in a single line

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coming as God first created them argues that the One who first created and gave life can resurrect; the Quran repeats this argument against resurrection-deniers.
rows.anchor: just as He created and gave life to people initially, so too does He have the power to give them new life

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, people come as first created in the sense of being alone, naked, and without worldly support.
rows.anchor: they come to Him in the same state as that in which He initially created them, that is, alone, bare, and without any worldly support

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The verse counters Makkan social superiority: wealth and status distinctions will disappear on the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: indicating that all such worldly distinctions will be absent on that Day

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The tryst is the time when the Resurrection and Gathering warned of by the prophets comes to pass.
rows.anchor: The tryst refers to the time when the Resurrection and Gathering of which the prophets warned will come to pass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is each person's record of earthly deeds, not the Quran or sacred scripture generally; it comprehensively witnesses human acts.
rows.anchor: The Book here refers not to the Quran or sacred scripture in general, but to the record of deeds done in life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere the record is written by angelic guardians, attached to each person's neck, and delivered to the right hand for favorable judgment or left for punishment.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere this book is described as being written by noble guardians, understood to mean angels

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The guilty regret having squandered their lives and fear punishment and public disgrace when the record exposes evil deeds they had hidden from others.
rows.anchor: The guilty express regret for having squandered their lives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's judgment wrongs no one: punishment is only for deeds people freely chose to commit.
rows.anchor: the punishment meted out to individuals on this Day will be only for what their own hands have sent forth

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: A ḥadīth says God admits no one to Garden or Fire until all interpersonal claims are fairly settled, with dues repaid in either direction.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states that God will place no one in either the Garden or the Fire until all accounts between human beings are fairly settled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read with v. 47, this assures that no one escapes judgment: no one is left behind, and every deed appears in the record; the same verb ghādara links the claims.
rows.anchor: same verb, ghādara, to mean

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brief Adam account recalls the fuller Quranic creation and fall narrative and admonishes wealthy, proud Makkans: Iblīs's refusal likewise sprang from pride and false superiority.
rows.anchor: Iblīs’s refusal to prostrate before Adam was based similarly on pride and a false sense of superiority to Adam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that all angels prostrated except Iblīs suggests he was an angel, although the verse immediately identifies him as a jinn, prompting scholarly debate.
rows.anchor: That all the angels prostrated, save Iblīs, suggests that Iblīs himself was among the angels

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: One view says Iblīs was a jinn, not an angel: angels are protected from disobedience, whereas his jinn nature explains his refusal and deviation.
rows.anchor: since angels are protected against any disobedience toward God

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Another view holds that Iblīs was an angel, perhaps their head, transformed after disobedience from an angel into a satan and thus a jinn.
rows.anchor: Others hold that he was indeed an angel, perhaps the head of the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblīs's progeny are evil jinn and satans who seek to lead humans astray.
rows.anchor: His progeny refers to the evil jinn and the satans mentioned elsewhere in the Quran

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Taking Satan or his minions as protectors means obeying them instead of God.
rows.anchor: meaning that they obey them instead of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan and his progeny are human beings' enemies, as the Quran repeatedly calls Satan a manifest enemy.
rows.anchor: They are the enemies of human beings, like Satan himself, who is repeatedly described as a manifest enemy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The evil exchange trades God's true protection for Satan's illusory protection.
rows.anchor: The evil exchange is the exchange of God’s true protection

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Because satans did not witness or partner in creating the heavens and earth, it is illogical to treat them as God's partners in worship.
rows.anchor: since the satans were not partners with God in creation, it is illogical to consider them as partners with God in being worshipped

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The satans' absence even from their own creation underscores that they are merely creatures.
rows.anchor: That they were not witness even to their own creation emphasizes that they are themselves mere creatures

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God challenges those who associated partners with Him to call them for intercession or aid as a rebuke; the alleged partners abandon, disown, or cannot help them.
rows.anchor: to intercede for them or to help them

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Mawbiq may mean a place of destruction or a valley of Hell into which idolaters are cast.
rows.anchor: between them may refer to a place of destruction

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, mawbiq may mean the enmity that becomes manifest between idolaters and the partners they ascribed to God.
rows.anchor: Others suggest that mawbiq may refer here to the enmity that will manifest itself

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the gulf the vast barzakh between Makkan idolaters who associated angels with God, in Hell, and the angels in the highest celestial realm.
rows.anchor: Still others interpret the gulf between them as referring to the vast intermediate expanse

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: The guilty are certain the Fire is their destiny; because ẓannū can mean “think,” al-Rāzī alternatively says they may see it far away yet imagine it near from its roaring and fear an immediate fall.
rows.anchor: That the guilty know they shall fall into it means that they are certain that it is their destiny

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: They cannot escape or change course because angels are driving them forward toward the Fire.
rows.anchor: they have no means of changing their course, since they are being driven forward by the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's many kinds of parables serve human moral and religious instruction.
rows.anchor: that is, for the moral and religious instruction of human beings

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Bḍ
rows.claim: Human beings are contentious because they vainly argue against prophets and messengers on false grounds; the discussion continues in v. 56.
rows.anchor: vainly opposing and arguing against the prophets and messengers sent to them

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: People await whether the same worldly destruction that befell earlier peoples will come upon them; the Quran says God's way with disbelievers does not change.
rows.anchor: they wait to see if the same worldly destruction that befell earlier peoples will be visited upon them as well

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The punishment arriving face-to-face likely means punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The punishment that may come upon them face-to-face likely refers to punishment in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Qubulan may instead mean that punishment comes suddenly, as divine punishment often does.
rows.anchor: Face-to-face translates qubulan, which may also mean “suddenly”

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: With alternate voweling, qabalan can mean “in the future.”
rows.anchor: It is also possible to read this word with alternate voweling as qabalan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mursalīn denotes all divine message-bearers, including both messengers (rusul) and prophets (anbiyāʾ); their charge is glad tidings and warning.
rows.anchor: denotes all message bearers from God, including both messengers

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Commentators call mocking God's signs and warnings the worst kind of denial.
rows.anchor: commentators note is the worst kind of denial

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Mockery also manifests profound ignorance and hardness of heart.
rows.anchor: an attitude that manifests their profound ignorance and hardness of heart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question “Who does greater wrong than” recurs, including the identical wording at 32:22, often about those denying God's signs.
rows.anchor: The rhetorical question beginning Who does greater wrong than is repeated throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coverings over hearts and deafness in ears parallel 6:25 and 2:7; spiritual incapacity makes the signs' guidance ineffective, as also stated in 2:6.
rows.anchor: Those who are spiritually “covered” or “deaf” are impervious to the guidance offered by God’s signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's forgiving mercy explains why He does not immediately punish the disbelievers; their appointed death or destruction leaves time to repent and mend their ways.
rows.anchor: God does not take the disbelievers to task immediately, because He is Forgiving and Possessed of Mercy

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Some understand this as a specific warning to the hostile Makkans, whom God did not punish immediately.
rows.anchor: According to some, this verse is understood to be a warning to the disbelievers in Makkah specifically

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The appointed tryst may mean their coming to judgment on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: may refer either to their coming to judgment on the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, the tryst may be the Battle of Badr in 2/624, when many Makkans, including prominent opponents, were killed.
rows.anchor: or to the Battle of Badr (2/624; R, Z), during which many Makkans

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: After the appointed tryst, they will have no refuge or means to escape God's punishment.
rows.anchor: they shall find no refuge or means of deliverance from God’s Punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly says towns were destroyed for disbelief and wrongdoing; Makkan sūrahs' examples are widely understood as warnings to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: it is widely understood that these were intended as warnings for the Quraysh of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God appoints a specific, known-only-to-Him time for destruction that cannot be advanced or delayed, as the Prophet is told to warn the Makkans.
rows.anchor: He has appointed a specific time, known only to Him, for their punishment, and it cannot be advanced or delayed
